text: REST stands for Representational State Transfer. It's not a protocol or a piece of software — it's an architectural style, a set of conventions for designing APIs. Most APIs you'll touch in this course, including AI provider APIs, call themselves RESTful.

Three ideas make an API RESTful. Resources: everything is a noun, addressed by its own URL. Statelessness: every request carries everything the server needs. Standard verbs: REST reuses GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE instead of inventing action names.

Here's resource-based design in practice. The user with id 42 lives at slash users slash 42. Order 1001 lives at slash orders slash 1001. Compare that to an older style where the action is crammed into the URL instead of the resource living there cleanly.

Statelessness is the one that surprises people. Every single request carries its own auth token, even if you sent one five seconds ago. The server remembers nothing about you between calls — which means any server in a pool can handle any request.
Resources, statelessness, standard verbs — that's REST. Next lesson, we go deep on those verbs themselves: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, and the status codes that tell you what actually happened.
